text:
Alex: Quick sync — I ran a sizing sweep to compare streaming chat vs sync completions. Observed p99 tail blowups when we increase microbatch size for streaming. Hoping for quick triage.
Maya: can you paste the numbers/config?
Alex: sure — quick summary first: model=redwood-xl-8k, hw=p4d.2x, clients synthetic chat mix vs sync bulk gen. mb sizes tried: 1,4,8,16.
Alex: results snapshot:
```
config: model=redwood-xl-8k, hw=p4d.2x, mb=[1,4,8,16]
streaming p95/p99 ms: mb1: 42/120, mb4: 48/180, mb8: 55/300, mb16: 62/520
sync completions p95/p99 ms: mb1: 60/130, mb4: 75/160, mb8: 90/200, mb16: 110/250
throughput (tokens/s per GPU): streaming: mb1=400, mb4=950, mb8=1200, mb16=1400
sync: mb1=300, mb4=1400, mb8=2200, mb16=2700
kv-miss-rate: streaming: mb1=2%, mb4=3.8%, mb8=6.5%, mb16=9.4%
kernel-fallbacks: small-batch kernel preferred until mb>=8 where we start seeing int8/large-batch kernels with higher tail work
```
Maya: interesting — streaming p99 jumps much faster than sync. Your throughput gain for streaming flattens after mb8 while tail explodes.
Juan: this smells like KV cache thrash + heavier tail work on large-batch kernels. Do you have eviction metrics?
Alex: yes — ran the perf collector:
```
$ perf-collect --pool=streaming --range=30m --mb=16
KV cache evictions/s: 2.1 -> 15.3 (mb1 -> mb16)
KV spill-to-host (MB/s): 0.0 -> 12.4
Kernel tail-time (ms): median 6 -> p99 480
```
Ciara: spill-to-host explains p99. When mb gets larger we keep more KV per batch but collisions + longer per-batch compute means other requests wait and KV entries get evicted/written back. Streaming is more sensitive because of frequent small requests and handshake ordering.
Maya: also check handshake amplification — streaming has extra per-request IO that can get amplified when mb groups heterogeneous sequence lengths.
Alex: I grabbed traces. observed many small inflight streaming requests trigger kernel selection that switches to large-batch optimized GEMM which has a longer tail for small prefixes. On top of that, KV misses cause async loads that block token emission.
Juan: proposed mitigations: 1) cap streaming mb_size to 8 as a short-term SLO fix; 2) bump KV cache allocation for streaming pool or tune eviction policy to favor short-lived prefixes; 3) force small-batch kernel for streaming via kernel-hint for mb<=8; 4) experiment with prefetching KV for expected prefixes.
Ciara: +1 to cap and kernel-hint. We should avoid forcing small-batch kernel everywhere — costs throughput for sync completions. Instead route streaming to a low-latency pool with smaller mb cap.
Alex: ran a follow-up with kernel-hint forced to small-batch for streaming mb8: p99 dropped from 300ms -> 95ms, throughput dropped ~12% but p95/p99 SLOs met.
```
follow-up: streaming mb8 forced-small-kernel: p95/p99 58/95 ms, tok/s -12%
```
Maya: that's promising. For Dedicated customers we can offer a low-latency streaming profile (pool-level config) that pins kernel and kv-size.
Juan: longer term: adapt kernel-selection using tail-aware cost model — prefer lower p99 even if p50 slightly worse for request types labeled latency-sensitive. Also consider better KV prefetch heuristics and per-customer warm caches.
Ciara: action items:
- Alex: run a 24h canary with streaming pool cap=8 + kernel-hint, collect p50/p95/p99 + kv-eviction traces. (Alex)
- Maya: add an ops knob in the console: streaming profile toggle (low-latency / high-throughput) + explain tradeoffs. (Maya)
- Juan: prototype tail-aware kernel selector that adds a p99 penalty term. (Juan)
Alex: started the canary, pushing logs to perf-bucket. Will post TL;DR in 2 runs.
perf-bot: Canary deployed to pool=streaming-lowlat at 3123456820 :rocket:
Maya: sweet. if the canary holds we cut a short RFC for console option.
Ciara: thanks team — this is a nice concrete route to keep streaming SLOs predictable without hampering bulk throughput. :thumbsup:
